1 · Read the explanation.
What the verb adds to the words

Reporting verbs carry judgement. He said the campaign worked is neutral. He claimed tells the reader the evidence has not been shown. He insisted tells them somebody was arguing back. He admitted tells them the statement cost him something. He denied tells them there was an accusation. Choosing the verb is the main way a reporter shows their reading of a story without giving an opinion.

The patterns matter as much as the meanings. Most take that: argue, claim, insist, point out, announce, indicate, confirm. A group needs a person before that: tell, remind, assure, inform — he assured us that, never he assured that. Admit, deny, report and suggest take -ing or that, and never an infinitive. Promise, refuse, offer, agree, threaten take to + verb. Invite, remind, advise, persuade, ask take a person and then to + verb.

Prepositions. Insist on doing, apologise for doing, accuse somebody of doing, congratulate somebody on doing. The verb after a preposition is always -ing, as in lesson 34.

Backshift still applies. The tense rules from lesson 37 do not change: He admitted that he had taken it. With a present reporting verb, nothing shifts: The company claims the campaign was a success keeps whatever tense was used.

Choosing badly is a real error. He denied that he was late and he admitted that he was late describe two different events; a translator who picks the wrong one has changed the story.

The commonest errors at this level
  • He denied to take it — deny never takes an infinitive.
  • She suggested to go — suggest takes -ing or that.
  • He assured that it was safe — the person is missing.
  • He insisted to pay — insist on paying.
  • He accused me to steal it — accused me of stealing it.

Two things to watch

1 — Admit, deny, suggest, report: no infinitive, ever. Use -ing or that.

2 — Ask what the verb tells the reader to believe. If you would not vouch for the statement, claim. If evidence points that way, indicate. If the speaker was contradicting somebody, insist.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Choosing the verb, then the pattern

The words: “We did not take the money — and anyway it was never ours.” — said by the teenagers, after being called heroes.

Step 1 — what was the speaker doing? Rejecting a description of themselves. That is deny, not say.

Step 2 — which pattern does that verb take? Deny takes that or an -ing form, never an infinitive: They denied acting heroically or They denied that they had acted heroically.

Step 3 — the second half is different. They are correcting an assumption, so: and pointed out that the money was not theirs.

Step 4 — check the backshift. The reporting verb is past, so the reported verb moves back: was → had been, unless the fact is still true, in which case either is acceptable.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
Six patterns

verb + that: say, claim, argue, insist, point out, announce, warn, indicate, confirm, deny, admit — She argued that it was cheaper. verb + person + that: tell, remind, assure, inform, warn — He assured us that it was safe. verb + -ing: admit, deny, report, suggest, recommend — They denied taking it. verb + to + infinitive: promise, refuse, offer, agree, threaten — He refused to comment. verb + person + to + infinitive: invite, remind, advise, persuade, warn, ask — She reminded me to email him. verb + preposition + -ing: insist on, apologise for, accuse somebody of — He insisted on paying.

Several verbs appear in more than one row, and both are correct: admitted that he took it and admitted taking it; warned that the road was closed and warned us to leave.

The verb is the reporter's opinion

Said reports the words and nothing more. Every other verb tells the reader what to think of them. Claimed signals that the statement is unproved and possibly false. Argued says reasons were given. Insisted says it was said against doubt or resistance. Pointed out says it was true and corrected an assumption — you cannot point out something false. Admitted concedes something that costs the speaker; denied rejects a charge; indicated is hedged and usually means the evidence suggests it rather than that anybody said it outright.

This is why He claimed the road was closed and He pointed out that the road was closed report the same words and take opposite positions on them. In journalism the choice is a professional decision; in an essay, using claimed for a source you accept, or pointed out for one you dispute, undercuts your own argument.

Errors to watch: He suggested me to check → suggested checking or suggested that I check · She said me → told me · He insisted to pay → insisted on paying · They accused me to take it → accused me of taking it · He denied to take it → denied taking it.

One story, reported properly

Take something that happened near you and write it the way a news service would: claims attributed, doubts marked, nothing invented.

The brief

Report a real local story — a decision, a campaign, a dispute, an opening or a closure. Say what happened, report what at least two sides said, and use your reporting verbs to show which claims are supported and which are not. Do not give your own opinion in the first three paragraphs.

1 · Read the model report.
Model · a news report in four paragraphs

The city has announced that the bus route through the old market will be closed to traffic from September. Officials say the road is unsafe; two collisions were recorded there last year, and the pavement is one metre wide.

Traders argue that the closure will finish the market. One stallholder pointed out that eighty per cent of his customers arrive by that bus, and that no alternative stop has been announced. The transport department has assured traders that a new stop will open within two hundred metres of the square, but it has not confirmed when. A spokesperson claimed that similar closures elsewhere in the country had increased footfall by a fifth; the figure comes from the department’s own report, and the two towns named in it are both larger than this one.

Not everybody in the market agrees. Three younger traders said they had wanted the road closed for years, and one admitted that she had signed the residents’ petition against her own association. The campaigners deny being funded by the developers who own the corner building, and no evidence has been produced that they are.

What is still unconfirmed is the thing everybody is arguing about: whether the new stop will be in place before the road closes. Until the department answers that, both sides are describing different Septembers.
